questions.q: Which climate category does the Court give for the Naoussa PDO in northern Greece?
questions.exp: Naoussa lies on the eastern foothills of Mount Vermio in Macedonia, with cold winters that can bring snow, warm summers and a long dry autumn for the late-ripening Xinomavro, so the Court calls it continental. The Court gives Santorini, out in the Aegean, a warm Mediterranean climate instead.

questions.q: Sigalas, the one Greek producer the Court names, makes its wine on which island?
questions.exp: Domaine Sigalas, founded in 1991 at Oia in the north of the island, makes Assyrtiko on Santorini's volcanic soils, and its single-vineyard Kavalieros set a modern standard for site-driven Assyrtiko. Crete is home to Vidiano and Liatiko, Samos to Muscat and Kefalonia to Robola.

questions.q: Naoussa Xinomavro arrives at the table with firm tannin and high acidity. Which dish does the Court's pairing advice point to?
questions.exp: The Court calls Naoussa Xinomavro a bold, often oak-aged red that needs meat or animal fat, lamb or beef, to tame its tannin, so roast lamb is the answer. Seafood, roasted fish and fresh cheeses are the Court's partners for Santorini Assyrtiko, the island's crisp, mineral white.

questions.q: Greece lies in southern Europe between two seas: the Aegean to the east and which sea to the west?
questions.exp: The Ionian Sea washes western Greece and islands such as Kefalonia, home of Robola, while the Aegean to the east holds the Cyclades, Santorini among them. The Court places Greece between the two, and the sea's moderating influence reaches most Greek vineyards, which seldom lie far from the coast.

questions.q: What type of soil does the Court give for Santorini's vineyards?
questions.exp: Santorini is the rim of a volcano that collapsed into the sea, and its vines grow in layers of ash, pumice and lava with almost no clay. Phylloxera cannot survive in that soil, so the vines grow on their own roots, and the porous pumice soaks up the night's sea humidity through the dry summer.

questions.q: Why does the Court say Santorini's vines are trained into the shape of baskets?
opts: To keep phylloxera out of the soil
To shield the grapes from strong winds
To raise the yield of each vine
questions.exp: The kouloura coils each vine into a low basket on the ground, with the bunches inside, sheltered from the strong summer meltemi off the Aegean, from blown sand and from the sun. It has nothing to do with phylloxera, which the volcanic soil keeps away by itself, and it makes every harvest a hand harvest.

questions.q: Agiorgitiko, one of the Court's two Greek reds, is the grape of which PDO?
questions.exp: Nemea, in Corinthia in the north-eastern Peloponnese, is Agiorgitiko alone, a deep, plummy red with soft tannin. The exam likes to swap the two great Greek reds: Xinomavro belongs to Naoussa in Macedonia, Rapsani blends it with Krassato and Stavroto, and Amyndeon uses it for rosé and sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which pair of traits does the Court say marks Santorini Assyrtiko in the glass?
opts: Low acidity and an oily texture
questions.exp: The Court calls Santorini Assyrtiko a classic white with intense acidity and minerality: the grape holds its acid even when it ripens to high sugar in the island's heat, and the volcanic soil and salt air add a saline, flinty edge. That is why the Court sets it beside seafood, roasted fish and fresh cheeses.
